name: Uddyotakara
dates_notes: Dated by his explicit replies to Diṅnāga (c. 480 CE) and by Dharmakīrti's (c. 600–660 CE) replies in turn; Vidyabhusana 1920 and Matilal 1977 converge on the late sixth or early seventh century. Uddyotakara identifies himself as a Pāśupata Śaiva in the colophon of the Vārttika.

lineage_polemical.note: The Nyāya-Vārttika is largely structured as a reply to Dignāga's Pramāṇa-Samuccaya: Uddyotakara defends the Naiyāyika four-pramāṇa scheme against the pramāṇa-dvaya thesis, the savikalpaka-pratyakṣa analysis against the kalpanā-apoḍha account, and jāti-realism against the apoha-vāda. The Nyāya–Buddhist epistemological exchange has Dignāga as one canonical pole.

Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇa-Vārttika is the Buddhist counter-reply to Uddyotakara's Nyāya-Vārttika: the Naiyāyika defense of the four pramāṇas, of jāti-realism, and of the Naiyāyika analysis of the inferential mark is engaged point-by-point and answered from the developed Buddhist-pramāṇa standpoint.

core_thesis: Uddyotakara’s *Nyāya-Vārttika* defends Vātsyāyana’s reading of the *Nyāya-Sūtra* in sustained engagement with Dignāga’s Buddhist epistemology. It develops Nyāya treatments of inference, fallacious reasons, and the relevance of similar and dissimilar instances. Against *apoha* accounts of meaning, Uddyotakara defends a realist account of universals and their role in cognition. He also argues that testimony is an independent means of knowledge rather than reducible to inference. The *Vārttika* preserves and extends debates over perception, language, and external objects that were central to early medieval Indian philosophy. It became a principal object of commentary for Vācaspati Miśra and Udayana and helped establish the technical vocabulary of mature Old Nyāya.

engaged_works.title: Nyaya-Varttika
engaged_works.composition_dates_notes: Composition dated by explicit Diṅnāga-replies and by Dharmakīrti's later engagement.
engaged_works.ascription_notes: Securely authored sub-commentary on Vātsyāyana's Bhāṣya; its colophon identifies Uddyotakara as a Pāśupata.
engaged_works.summary: *Vārttika*-style sub-commentary on Vātsyāyana's *Nyāya-Sūtra-Bhāṣya*, working through the *Sūtra* and *Bhāṣya* together. The polemical occasion is Diṅnāga's *Pramāṇa-Samuccaya* (esp. chapter 1 on *pratyakṣa* and chapter 5 on *apoha*): Uddyotakara opens with a *maṅgala* whose explicit purpose is to defend the *Bhāṣya* against the criticisms it has accumulated. The bulk of the polemical work happens at three loci. *Nyāya-Vārttika* on [NS 1.1.4](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/1.1.4) on *pratyakṣa* — Uddyotakara reformulates the perceptual definition to handle Diṅnāga's objections about *kalpanāpoḍha* (free-of-conceptual-construction) perception (against [*Pramāṇa-Samuccaya* 1.3–4](cite://dignaga/pramana-samuccaya/1.3-4)). *Nyāya-Vārttika* on [NS 1.1.5](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/1.1.5) (with [NS 1.2.4–9](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/1.2.4-9)) on *anumāna* — the *tri-rūpa-liṅga* analysis is reset on a realist footing and the *hetv-ābhāsa* fivefold typology (*asiddha*, *viruddha*, *anaikāntika*, *prakaraṇa-sama*, *kālātīta*) is developed. *Nyāya-Vārttika* on [NS 2.2.66](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/2.2.66) on *jāti* — the *apoha*-vs-realist-universal debate (against [*Pramāṇa-Samuccaya* 5.1–11](cite://dignaga/pramana-samuccaya/5.1-11)) is centered here in its classical form. The *Vārttika*'s technical achievement is to absorb Buddhist epistemological pressure without conceding the realist ontology; its historical achievement is to fix the form in which the *Sūtra*-*Bhāṣya* are read in the medieval Nyāya school.
